hero.text: AQA publishes its specimen papers, mark schemes and examiner reports free of charge. Those are linked here as they are. Beside them is an original RCF practice paper, clearly labelled as practice material.

blocks.title: How papers are handled here
text: **Official papers are linked, never copied.** AQA owns its question papers, source material, mark schemes and examiner reports. Every official item below opens on aqa.org.uk or AQA's own file store. This site hosts no copy of any of them and links to no paper-sharing site.
**RCF papers are labelled on every page that carries them.** They are written by RCF English in the format of the examination. They are not past papers, not specimen papers, and not endorsed by AQA.

**RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by AQA.** AQA is the copyright owner of its assessment materials and the owner of its name and logo, neither of which appears on any RCF material.

blocks.title: Examiner reports are the most under-used free resource
text: AQA publishes an examiner report for each series alongside the papers and mark schemes on its [assessment resources page](https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/english/gcse/english-8700/assessment-resources). They set out what candidates actually did well and badly that year, question by question.
Filter that page by *Examiner reports* to find them. Reading one before your next timed paper is the most direct guidance available on where marks are lost, and almost no student does it.

blocks.title: More papers, and the other boards
text: RCF Model Paper 1 is deliberately the only one so far. Its format is being checked before it becomes the template for a Paper 2 model paper and for the other boards.
Pearson Edexcel, OCR and Eduqas GCSE English Language will follow, each with the same structure: verified official links first, then an original model paper once the template is settled.

items.q: Where can I get AQA English Language past papers free?
a: From AQA's own assessment resources page for specification 8700, which publishes past question papers, mark schemes and examiner reports free of charge. It is linked at the top of this page. The most recent series are sometimes restricted to teachers for a period before being released publicly.

items.q: Why does this site not host the papers itself?
a: Because AQA owns them, along with the copyright in the source texts inside them, much of which is licensed from other publishers. Copying an examination paper onto another website is a breach of copyright whatever the intention. Linking to the official page is lawful and keeps you on the current version.

items.q: Is the RCF model paper a real AQA paper?
a: No, and it is labelled as practice material on every page. It follows AQA's published structure - the same durations, sections, question types and marks - using a source and questions written by RCF English that have never appeared in an examination. Use it for practice and use AQA's specimen paper to see the genuine standard.

items.q: How should I use a past paper?
a: Under timed conditions, once, without the mark scheme open. Mark it afterwards against the official mark scheme, then read the examiner report for that series. Doing three papers casually teaches less than doing one properly and marking it honestly.

blocks.heading: How to use a practice question properly

items.title: Time it, even when it is short
text: A 10-minute question answered in 25 minutes tells you nothing about what you can do in the examination. Set a timer and stop when it goes.

items.title: Do not read the model answer first
text: Reading a model answer before attempting the question feels like learning and is not. You will recognise the moves without being able to make them.

items.title: Mark against the moves, not the content
text: Your answer will not match the model, and it should not. Ask instead: did I quote briefly, name an effect, and develop past the explanation? Those are the transferable parts.

items.title: Redo one paragraph
text: Not the whole answer - one paragraph, rewritten with the missing move added. Ten minutes of that is worth more than a second full attempt.

blocks.heading: A self-marking checklist that works for any reading answer
items: Did I answer from the lines or the source the question named?
Is every quotation short enough to sit inside my own sentence?
Have I named an effect on the reader for each one?
Have I developed at least one point past the explanation?
Could any paragraph of mine have been written about a different text? If so, it is too general.
Did I finish within the time the marks deserve?

blocks.title: Before you start

blocks.heading: Source A
text: **This extract is from the opening of a novel. It is an original passage written by RCF English for this practice paper.** The narrator, Ines, has returned to the island where she grew up to close up her grandmother's house.

parts.heading: From The Quiet Season (original RCF source)
text: **1** The ferry came in past the breakwater at ten past four, an hour late, and by then the light had already begun to go. Ines stood at the rail with her bag between her feet and watched the harbour arrange itself: the same two cranes, the same yellow chandlery with its shutters down, the same three boats hauled out on the slipway with weed drying on their keels. Nothing had been repainted. Nothing had been taken away. She had expected to feel something at the sight of it and she felt, instead, a kind of administrative relief, as though she had checked a list.

**8** The road up from the harbour was steeper than she remembered, which she knew was not the road's doing. Halfway along it she stopped, ostensibly to change hands on the bag, and stood breathing in the smell of the place - salt, diesel, and underneath both of them something green and rotting that she had never been able to name and had never smelled anywhere else in her life. Twenty-two years, and her body had recognised it before she had. She found she was angry about that, in a small way, the way you are angry at a door that sticks.

**15** The house was at the top, behind the church, with its back to the weather. The key was where it had always been kept, under the third stone, and the stone came up as easily as if someone had lifted it that morning. Inside, the hall was cold in the particular way of a house that has been empty rather than merely unheated - cold all the way through, cold in the walls. Ines put down her bag. In the kitchen the clock had stopped at twenty past nine and she did not know, standing there, whether that was morning or evening, or how many months ago, and it seemed to her suddenly a serious question, one she ought to be able to answer.

**23** She went from room to room turning on lights. Most of them worked. In the back bedroom the bulb had gone, and she stood in the doorway looking at the shape of the bed in the last of the daylight and decided she would deal with it tomorrow, and then went on standing there. Outside, the wind had got up and was working at the shutters, and the sound was so exactly the sound of her childhood that she had to remind herself she was not expected anywhere, that nobody downstairs was waiting to hear her come down, that the house was hers now in the flat legal sense that meant nothing at all.

**31** She slept that night in the front room with her coat over the blanket, and woke twice, and the second time lay listening to the sea and thinking, quite clearly and without any distress: I have made a mistake, and I am going to stay.

blocks.heading: Section A: Reading
text: Answer **all** questions in this section. You are advised to spend about 45 minutes on this section. **[40 marks]**

parts.heading: Question 1
text: Read again the first part of the source, **lines 1 to 7**.
List **four** things from this part of the text about the harbour. **[4 marks]**

parts.heading: Question 2
text: Look in detail at **lines 8 to 14** of the source.
How does the writer use language here to describe Ines's return to the island? **[8 marks]**
You could include the writer's choice of:
bullets: words and phrases
language features and techniques
sentence forms

parts.heading: Question 3
text: You now need to think about the **whole** of the source.
This text is from the opening of a novel. How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader? **[8 marks]**
You could write about:
bullets: what the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning
how and why the writer changes this focus as the source develops
any other structural features that interest you

parts.heading: Question 4
text: Focus this part of your answer on the second part of the source, from **line 15 to the end**.
A student said: *"In this part of the extract the writer makes Ines seem detached from her own feelings, and that detachment is more affecting than open emotion would have been."*
To what extent do you agree? **[20 marks]**
In your response, you could:
bullets: write about your own impressions of Ines
evaluate how the writer has created these impressions
support your opinions with references to the text

blocks.heading: Section B: Writing
text: You are advised to spend about 45 minutes on this section. Write in full sentences. You are reminded of the need to plan your answer. You should leave enough time to check your work at the end.
**Question 5**
Your school or college is producing an anthology of new writing.
**Either:** Write a description of a building that has been left empty.
**Or:** Write the opening part of a story about someone returning to a place they left long ago.
*(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)* **[40 marks]**

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: This marking guide accompanies [RCF Model Paper 1](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/rcf-model-paper-1/), an original practice paper written by RCF English.

It is **not** an AQA mark scheme. The band descriptions below are RCF English's own plain-English account of how marks divide on this kind of question; no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced. For the authoritative standard, use AQA's specimen mark schemes and examiner reports, linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/).
RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by AQA.

blocks.heading: Question 1: four things about the harbour (4 marks)
text: One mark each, to a maximum of four. Accept any four separate points drawn from lines 1 to 7. Do not credit a fifth answer, and do not credit material from later in the source.
bullets: There were two cranes.
There was a yellow chandlery.
The chandlery's shutters were down.
Three boats were hauled out on the slipway.
The boats had weed drying on their keels.
Nothing had been repainted.
Nothing had been taken away.
The ferry came in past a breakwater.

blocks.heading: Question 2: language, lines 8 to 14 (8 marks)
text: AO2. Reward what a candidate says about the effect of the writer's choices, not the number of features named. A top-band answer analyses effects, selects a judicious range of short quotations and uses terminology accurately.

parts.heading: Indicative content
bullets: **"steeper than she remembered, which she knew was not the road's doing"** - the aside concedes her own ageing without stating it, so the reader infers what Ines will not say.
**"ostensibly to change hands on the bag"** - a single adverb admits the pretence; she is hiding the pause from herself as much as from anyone watching.
**"salt, diesel, and underneath both of them something green and rotting"** - the triple, moving from clean to unpleasant, mirrors the movement from surface memory to something less welcome.
**"she had never been able to name and had never smelled anywhere else in her life"** - the parallel clauses make the smell simultaneously unknowable and unique to this place.
**"her body had recognised it before she had"** - the split between body and self is the central idea of the paragraph, and it is delivered flatly, without imagery.

**"the way you are angry at a door that sticks"** - a deliberately small simile that reduces a large emotion to a domestic irritation, which characterises Ines as someone who scales her feelings down.

parts.heading: Bands, in plain English
bullets: **7-8** Detailed, perceptive analysis of effects; judicious short quotations; accurate terminology used where it helps.
**5-6** Clear explanation of effects; relevant quotations; terminology mostly accurate.
**3-4** Some understanding; features identified with simple comment on effect.
**1-2** Simple identification; effect asserted rather than explained.
**0** Nothing to reward.

blocks.heading: Question 3: structure (8 marks)
text: AO2, structure only. Do not reward language analysis here, however good. Reward what a candidate says about the order and shape of the whole extract.

parts.heading: Indicative content
bullets: **Opens outside and in motion** - the ferry, the harbour - before Ines is given any interior life, so the reader meets the place before the person.
**A steady inward movement** across the extract: harbour, road, house, room, bed. Each paragraph narrows the frame.
**The focus shifts from what she sees to what she cannot answer.** The stopped clock at line 20 turns an inventory of the house into a question about time.
**Withheld information** - twenty-two years, the grandmother, the reason for leaving - is released in fragments and never explained, which sustains interest.
**The wind and the shutters return** at line 27 as a sound from childhood, linking the end of the extract to a past the reader has not been shown.

**The final paragraph reverses the direction of the whole piece.** Everything has been about leaving and closing up; the last sentence is a decision to stay, and it arrives without warning or explanation.
**The last line is structurally two clauses in tension** - a mistake acknowledged and a decision made - so the extract ends by opening rather than resolving.

parts.heading: Bands, in plain English
bullets: **7-8** Detailed, perceptive understanding of structural features and analysis of their effects on the reader.
**5-6** Clear understanding; explains the effect of structural choices.
**3-4** Some understanding; identifies structural features with simple comment.
**1-2** Simple identification, or language analysis mistakenly offered as structure.
**0** Nothing to reward.

blocks.heading: Question 4: evaluation, line 15 to the end (20 marks)
text: AO4. Reward a clear position, developed judgements about how the writer creates the impressions, and references that support them. Agreement, disagreement and a qualified position are all equally acceptable.

parts.heading: Indicative content: agreeing with the student
bullets: Ines notices the cold "in the walls" but records no feeling about it - observation is used where emotion is expected.
The stopped clock provokes a factual question rather than grief, and the writer calls it "a serious question", which is comically inadequate to the situation and therefore affecting.
"decided she would deal with it tomorrow, and then went on standing there" - the sentence contradicts itself, showing feeling through behaviour rather than statement.
The legal vocabulary - "hers now in the flat legal sense that meant nothing at all" - holds the loss at arm's length by describing it administratively.
The final decision arrives "quite clearly and without any distress", and the absence of distress where the reader expects it is the extract's strongest effect.

parts.heading: Indicative content: qualifying or disagreeing
bullets: The detachment is not total: "she found she was angry about that" and "it seemed to her suddenly a serious question" both admit feeling directly.
The narration is close third person, so the reader is inside her perception throughout - a genuinely detached telling would not report her thoughts at all.
Some readers may find the flatness distancing rather than affecting, and a well-argued case that the writer withholds too much is entirely creditable.

parts.heading: Bands, in plain English
bullets: **16-20** Perceptive, detailed evaluation; a clear critical position developed with judicious references.
**11-15** Clear, relevant evaluation; a position taken and supported.
**6-10** Some evaluative comment; a position stated with limited support.
**1-5** Simple, limited comment; description of the text rather than judgement of it.
**0** Nothing to reward.

blocks.heading: Question 5: writing (40 marks)
text: 24 marks for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). Mark the two separately, and mark content first.

parts.heading: Content and organisation, 24 marks
bullets: **19-24** Convincing and compelling; tone, style and register matched to the task; a deliberate structure with varied paragraph lengths used for effect.
**13-18** Consistent and clear; the piece holds together; some conscious structural choices.
**7-12** Some success; a recognisable shape, with lapses.
**1-6** Simple, limited; little organisation.
**0** Nothing to reward.

parts.heading: Technical accuracy, 16 marks
bullets: **13-16** A wide range of sentence forms and vocabulary used for effect; punctuation, including the more demanding forms, used accurately; spelling secure.
**9-12** A range of sentence forms; mostly accurate punctuation and spelling.
**5-8** Some variety; errors present but meaning clear.
**1-4** Limited range; errors impede the reader.
**0** Not enough evidence to assess.

items.label: Original RCF model answer - the opening part of a story about returning
items.prompt: Write the opening part of a story about someone returning to a place they left long ago. (Original RCF practice task.)
sample: The bus put Yusuf down at the crossroads because the village stop had been discontinued, and the driver said this apologetically, as though it were a bereavement. It was, in a way. Yusuf said it was no trouble and stood in the road with his case until the bus had gone and the diesel had thinned out of the air.
Then there was only the sound of the wires.

He had forgotten the wires. They ran from the crossroads down the length of the lane on poles that leaned at various angles, and in any wind at all they made a low humming, not quite a note, that he had spent the whole of his childhood not hearing. He heard it now. He stood and listened to it for longer than a man ought to stand listening to overhead cables, and thought: this is the sound I have been trying to remember for eleven years, and I did not know it was a sound.

The lane was narrower than it had been. That was the trees, which had gone on growing while he had been elsewhere, doing that quietly and without asking anyone. The hedges had closed in until two people could not have passed without one of them turning sideways, and he found he minded this out of all proportion, as though the lane had been asked to wait and had failed to.

At the bend he could see the roof of the house. He had rehearsed this on the bus - had decided he would look at it steadily, take it in, and go on walking - and he did none of those things. He put his case down in the road and looked at the roof and thought about nothing at all for some considerable time, and a woman he did not recognise came past with a dog and said good afternoon, and he said good afternoon, and neither of them stopped.

When she had gone he picked up the case. The gate was shut. Of course it was shut; he had shut it himself, on a Tuesday, in the rain, and had not once in eleven years thought about the fact that a gate he closed had stayed closed the entire time without him.
notes: **Content and organisation, top band.** One change only - a man walks from a crossroads to a gate - and the whole interest is in what he notices. There is no plot and no twist, which is exactly what *the opening part of a story* invites.

**Deliberate structure.** Six paragraphs of markedly different length. The second is one sentence: *Then there was only the sound of the wires.* It is the shortest thing on the page and it turns the piece from arrival into memory.
**A shape that returns.** The case is put down in paragraph five and picked up in paragraph six, which closes the passage without ending the story.

**Range and accuracy (AO6).** Sentence forms vary from six words to fifty. The dash, the semicolon and the parenthetical dashes in paragraph five are all used correctly. Vocabulary is precise rather than elaborate - *discontinued*, *thinned*, *out of all proportion* - which is what range means at this level.

**Emotion carried by behaviour, not statement.** He *minded this out of all proportion*; he *did none of those things*; the final sentence measures eleven years by a closed gate. Nowhere does the piece say that he is sad.
**The last line opens.** He has picked up the case and the gate is still shut. The reader knows exactly what happens next and is not shown it.
